cells.tense: Right now you are holding the pen and the direction is yours.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Before you move on the next decision, take ten minutes to look at it as if you had just arrived. Ask one question whose answer you genuinely want. Then choose.
cells.core:
You can move, and choose which way, without jamming the two together. The engine is running here without a hand welded to it, and you test a direction by taking a step rather than arguing for it. Watch that keep working. What you find out while moving is information, not a detour, and the moves still get made.

This week, give the fresh look a little more room. Before you act on something, spend ten minutes on it the way a newcomer would, ask one question whose answer you genuinely want, and act after that. Direction doesn't weaken for being looked at. A course you can see is easier to hold than one you can only defend.

cells.verb: cut through inertia and set the direction by moving first

cells.tense: By the time the move is over you already know how the next three go.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Take one decision you are facing and cut straight to what it actually turns on. Write the single fact that settles it. Then act on that fact before you think about it again.
cells.core:
The charging has outrun the steering. You move and the momentum picks the way, so you are rarely standing where you are — already into the next move, already beyond the next three, faster than anyone can answer. The force is real and it works. It is just going where the speed takes it instead of where you point it.

Here is a still frame for it. Before the next decision, take the speed you already have and use it on one thing only: cut straight to what that decision turns on, name the single fact that settles it, and act on that before you think about it again. Nothing new is required. The speed is right. It needs a place to land.

cells.tense: You stood at that decision once and your hand is still on the door.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Find the change you keep meaning to start and work ten minutes on it today, ten tomorrow, for a week. Only the ten minutes. What comes after the week is a question for then.
cells.core:
The direction is clear and the engine will not turn over. You can see where to go plainly and the first move keeps not happening, so the decision sits out of reach while you wait to feel ready before you spend anything. Nothing is missing. The part of you that starts things is starved and waiting to be pulled through by motion.

Start with the hands, not the will. Find the change you keep meaning to start and work ten minutes on it today and ten tomorrow, for a week. Ten minutes is small enough to survive a tired day, and it turns the engine over without requiring that you feel decided. What comes after the week is a question for then, not tonight.

cells.tense: You are already steering this and would say it happens by itself.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Look at what you are still carrying because you once took it on. If it is finished, put it down this week. Let the done thing be done.
cells.core:
The hand on the wheel is yours and goes by another name. When a decision needs making, you make it, and afterwards it gets credited to the timing, the situation, the way things fell. The steering is happening all the same. What is missing is your name on it, and so the direction keeps getting credited to things that cannot steer.

A person gets their hand back in inches. Look at what you are still carrying only because you once took it on, and ask whether it still serves. If it is finished, put it down this week — not loudly, just where done things go. Letting go of what has ended is steering too, and the hand that does it is the one that picks what comes next. Own that inch and use it.
